basics.name: Idris Halloran
basics.label: Software engineer
basics.headline: I build payment systems.
basics.summary: Software engineer in Edinburgh. Payment systems, queues and the interfaces on top of them, each project led by the number it moved.
about: I started in warehouse software in Dundee, where a bug meant a lorry waiting in the yard. That is still how I think about latency.

From there I moved to card payments in Glasgow, then led an ingest pipeline through its awkward years. Since 2021 I have worked for myself from Leith, on two contracts a year. I take the ones where a slow page costs somebody money, because those teams already know which number matters.
Away from the desk I maintain Sandeel, a small feature-flag library, write a few essays a year and run badly along the Water of Leith.

projects.name: Fernhill Pay
projects.summary: A payments ledger for 9,000 small shops. One codebase from the till to the back office.

projects.problem: Checkout took 840 ms at the 95th percentile, and nobody could say where the time went. Shops with slow connections were giving up at the card step.
projects.solution: I traced one payment end to end before touching anything. Two thirds of the time was three lookups the ledger already had the answers to. I moved them into the write path, added one index and deleted a cache.
projects.result: Checkout now sits at 96 ms. The dashboards I used are part of the product, so the team sees a regression the day it ships.

projects.name: Harbourline
projects.summary: Route planning for a coastal courier fleet, replanned every time a van falls behind.
projects.imageAlt: Harbourline route planner: three delivery runs drawn along a coastline, with a list of runs beside the map
projects.problem: Drivers followed fixed rounds drawn up years ago. One late van meant phone calls, and a third of each day's distance was avoidable.
projects.solution: A routing service that replans every time a van falls behind, with rules the dispatchers can read and overrule. It ran beside the old rounds for a month before it replaced them.
projects.result: 31% fewer kilometres per parcel over twelve weeks, and the dispatch desk stopped starting at five in the morning.

projects.name: Sandeel
projects.summary: Flags without the meeting. Ship behind a switch and roll out by percentage.
projects.imageAlt: Sandeel feature flags: a list of flags with switches and percentage roll-out bars
projects.problem: Every release needed a meeting because nothing could be switched off once it was live.
projects.solution: A small library and one table: flags with owners, expiry dates and a percentage. No dashboard service to run, and no flag lives longer than a quarter without someone saying why.
projects.result: From merge to live in 11 seconds behind a flag. About forty teams use it, and three of them send patches.

metrics.label: From merge to live, behind a flag

projects.name: Stillwater
projects.summary: Latency you can read at a glance, for every region on one screen.
projects.imageAlt: Stillwater latency screen: an orange heat map of checkout latency over 24 hours, with four figures above it
projects.problem: The ingest pipeline fell over at 600 million requests a day and the fix on the table was a bigger cluster.
projects.solution: I rewrote the hot path in Go around one append-only log, with back-pressure instead of retries. We shipped it a region at a time, old and new side by side.
projects.result: 4.1 billion requests a day on fewer machines than before, and a latency screen people could read from across the room.

metrics.label: Requests a day, on one pipeline

projects.name: Bawbee
projects.summary: A current account that opens in the time it takes to boil a kettle.
projects.imageAlt: Bawbee banking app: three phone screens showing a balance, spending by month and savings pots
projects.problem: The app crashed most for the people with the oldest phones, which were also the customers it was built for.
projects.solution: I moved balance and payment state out of the screens into one store that both platforms share, then tested on the five worst phones we could buy.
projects.result: 99.9% of sessions end without a crash, up from 98.1%, and sign-up takes under four minutes.

metrics.label: Sessions that end without a crash

projects.name: Tidewatch
projects.summary: On-call rotas that nobody dreads, with every gap found before Friday.
projects.imageAlt: Tidewatch on-call rota: a week grid with primary and secondary shifts for five people
projects.problem: On-call rotas lived in a spreadsheet. Gaps were found on Friday afternoon, and the same two people took most of the night pages.
projects.solution: A scheduler that treats fairness as a constraint, not a favour, and flags a gap the moment it appears. Swaps take two taps.
projects.result: 62% fewer pages after midnight within a quarter, mostly because alerts finally reached someone who could fix the cause.

process.summary: No change without a number before it and the same number after. If it cannot be measured yet, that is the first job.

process.summary: A week of small merges behind a flag beats a month on a branch. Each one can be undone before lunch.

writing.title: The cheapest millisecond is the one you never spend
writing.summary: Most of a slow checkout is work nobody asked for. How to find it before you buy a bigger machine.

writing.title: What a double-entry ledger taught me about state
writing.summary: Never update a balance. Append what happened and let the sum speak.
writing.body:
Accountants solved a problem five hundred years ago that software teams rediscover every few years: if you overwrite a value, you lose the reason it changed.

## Never update a balance

A balance is a sum, not a fact. Store the movements and add them up. When the total looks wrong, the rows tell you which movement to question.

## Every entry has two sides

Money that leaves one account arrives in another. If the two sides do not match, the write fails. That single rule removed a whole class of bug from reconciliation.

## What it costs

More rows and the occasional slow sum. Both are easier to fix than a balance nobody can explain.

writing.title: Feature flags are a release tool, not a settings page
writing.summary: A flag older than a quarter is a bug with good manners.
writing.body:
A feature flag answers one question: is this code path on for this person yet. The trouble starts when it is asked to answer others.

## Give every flag an owner and a date

A flag without an expiry is a second configuration system that nobody designed. In Sandeel a flag past its date fails the build until someone extends it and says why.

## Roll out by percentage

One per cent for an hour tells you more than a week in staging. Watch the number you care about, then turn the dial.

## Delete the flag

The release is finished when the flag is gone, not when it reaches a hundred per cent.

writing.title: On-call is a design problem
writing.summary: If the same alert wakes two people in a month, the rota is not what needs fixing.
writing.body:
If the same alert wakes two people in a month, the rota is not what needs fixing.

## Count the pages, not the incidents

Incidents are what the company remembers. Pages are what people live through. Tidewatch started as a spreadsheet of who was woken and why.

## Fairness is a constraint

A schedule that leans on whoever complains least will lose them first. Make the load visible and the swaps easy.

## Send alerts to the cause

Most of the drop in night pages came from routing: the alert went to the team that could remove the reason for it.

faq.question: Do you work full time for one client?
faq.answer: During a contract, yes. I take two a year so that each gets my whole week.

faq.question: Can you work in our time zone?
faq.answer: I work UK hours and overlap comfortably with Europe and the east coast of the United States.

faq.question: Do you sign NDAs?
faq.answer: Yes, before the first call if you prefer. Case studies here were published with each client's agreement.

faq.question: What if the number does not move?
faq.answer: Then the audit says why, in writing, and you have paid for a fortnight rather than a rewrite.

faq.question: Would you consider a permanent role?
faq.answer: Occasionally. Staff or principal level, small team, a product where a slow page costs somebody money.
